title: Abu Bakr al-Baghdadi
subtitle: The quiet scholar who declared a terror state

package.intro: In July 2014, a man almost nobody had seen stood in a Mosul mosque and declared himself caliph. Abu Bakr al-Baghdadi turned a beaten insurgent group into a self-declared state that enslaved Yazidi women, filled mass graves and inspired attacks around the world. This documentary tells how he rose, how his state fell, and what it left behind.
facts: Born Ibrahim Awwad Ibrahim al-Badri in 1971 near Samarra, Iraq
Detained by US forces at Camp Bucca in 2004; released in December 2004
Became leader of the Islamic State of Iraq in May 2010
Announced the Islamic State of Iraq and al-Sham (ISIS) in April 2013
Group declared a 'caliphate' on 29 June 2014; he preached at Mosul's al-Nuri mosque on 4 July 2014
Attack on Sinjar began 3 August 2014; a UN commission found genocide against the Yazidis in June 2016
Mosul retaken July 2017; last territory lost at Baghouz, March 2019
Died during a US special forces raid in Barisha, Syria, 26–27 October 2019
package.sources: UN Independent International Commission of Inquiry on Syria ('They came to destroy', 2016), UNAMI/OHCHR report on mass graves in Iraq (2018), International Centre for the Study of Radicalisation at King's College London, Encyclopaedia Britannica, US Department of Defense statements (October 2019), William McCants's The ISIS Apocalypse.

sections.name: Cold open

lines.title: AL-BAGHDADI
lines.sub: The quiet scholar who declared a terror state

lines: On the fourth of July, 2014, a man in a black robe and a black turban climbed the pulpit of the Great Mosque of al-Nuri, in Mosul, Iraq's second-largest city.

lines.place: Great Mosque of al-Nuri · Mosul · Iraq

lines: Until that day, almost no one outside his movement knew what he looked like. Now, in front of the cameras, he claimed to be the leader of all Muslims: a caliph.

lines.label: foreigners who travelled to join his self-declared state

lines: Over the next few years, more than forty thousand people from around the world travelled to Iraq and Syria to join him.

lines.label: US reward offered for information leading to him

lines: The United States offered twenty-five million dollars for information leading to him.

lines.text: How did a shy scholar build a terror state?

lines: Abu Bakr al-Baghdadi turned a beaten insurgent group into a self-declared state that ruled millions of people and inspired murder around the world. This is how.

sections.name: The student
lines: He was born Ibrahim Awwad Ibrahim al-Badri in 1971, near Samarra, north of Baghdad, into a religious Sunni Muslim family.

lines.name: Ibrahim al-Badri
lines.role: Religious student from Samarra. Doctorate in Quranic studies.

lines: People who knew him as a young man described someone quiet and shy, who loved football and Quranic recitation. He studied in Baghdad and went on to earn a doctorate in Quranic studies.
Through the 1990s, under the dictatorship of Saddam Hussein, he lived modestly in Baghdad, studying and leading prayers at a local mosque.
Everything changed in 2003, when a US-led coalition invaded Iraq and overthrew Saddam. Sunni Arabs, who had dominated the old regime, lost power, and an insurgency spread.

sections.name: Prison and insurgency
lines: He helped found a small militant group. In early 2004 he was detained by American forces and held at Camp Bucca, a huge prison camp in the desert.

Bucca held thousands of men: committed militants, officers from Saddam's disbanded army, and ordinary people swept up in raids. Analysts later called it a meeting place for the future leaders of the Islamic State.
He was released in December 2004, judged a low-level threat. Later he joined the network of al-Qaeda in Iraq, the group founded by the Jordanian militant Abu Musab al-Zarqawi.
Al-Qaeda in Iraq bombed markets, mosques and crowds, deliberately targeting Shia Muslims to provoke a sectarian war. By 2006, Iraq was in exactly that kind of war.

sections.name: Taking over

lines.head: Insurgent leaders killed
lines.sub: Islamic State of Iraq loses its top two commanders

lines: By 2010 the group, now calling itself the Islamic State of Iraq, had been badly beaten by American troops and Sunni tribal fighters. In April, its top two leaders were killed.

lines.name: Abu Bakr al-Baghdadi
lines.role: Head of the Islamic State of Iraq. Rarely seen in public.

lines: In May 2010, the group named a new leader: a little-known scholar who now called himself Abu Bakr al-Baghdadi. Even many of his own fighters had never seen his face.
He rebuilt the group by killing rivals and informers, recruiting former officers of Saddam's army, and breaking members out of prisons.
Two events helped him. American troops left Iraq at the end of 2011. And across the border, Syria collapsed into civil war.

He sent fighters into Syria. In April 2013 he announced that his group now spanned both countries: the Islamic State of Iraq and al-Sham, known in English as ISIS. In early 2014, al-Qaeda's leadership publicly cut ties with him.

sections.name: The caliphate
lines: In June 2014, ISIS attacked Mosul. Iraqi army units many times larger than the attacking force collapsed and fled, abandoning weapons and vehicles.

On the twenty-ninth of June, the group declared a caliphate, a state claiming authority over all Muslims, with al-Baghdadi as its caliph. Muslim scholars and governments almost everywhere rejected the claim.
His sermon at al-Nuri was filmed and posted online. For years, it was the only time most of the world saw him speak.

lines.label: Raqqa · the group's capital in Syria

lines: At its height, the self-declared state held cities across Iraq and Syria, from Mosul to Raqqa, and ruled over millions of people.
It ran courts, collected taxes and printed school textbooks. It also staged public executions, punished people for smoking or playing music, and blew up ancient monuments.

sections.name: Genocide
lines: On the third of August, 2014, ISIS fighters attacked Sinjar, in northern Iraq, the homeland of the Yazidis, an ancient religious minority that ISIS regarded as unbelievers to be wiped out.
Thousands of Yazidi men and older women were killed. Thousands of women and girls were taken and sold into sexual slavery, and boys were forced to train as fighters.

lines.label: UN Commission of Inquiry on Syria · June 2016

lines: In 2016, a United Nations commission of inquiry found that ISIS had committed genocide against the Yazidis. Years later, thousands of the abducted were still missing.
Christians, Shia Muslims and other minorities were driven from their homes or killed. Sunni Muslims who resisted were killed too.

lines.label: mass graves found in areas ISIS held in Iraq (UN, 2018)

lines: In 2018 the United Nations reported more than two hundred mass graves in areas of Iraq that ISIS had held, which it said could contain up to twelve thousand victims.

sections.name: Terror abroad
lines: Al-Baghdadi's group recruited through slick videos and social media. Its films of hostages being murdered were made to shock the world, and to draw in new followers.
According to a 2018 study by King's College London, about forty-one thousand foreigners from some eighty countries joined it, including thousands of women and children.
It also directed or inspired attacks abroad. In November 2015, gunmen and suicide bombers killed one hundred and thirty people in Paris.
Brussels, Nice, Manchester and Sri Lanka followed, among many others. Far more people died in its attacks in Iraq, Syria, Afghanistan and Africa.

sections.name: The fall
lines: From 2014, a coalition led by the United States bombed ISIS, while Iraqi troops, Kurdish fighters and others fought it on the ground.
Mosul was retaken in July 2017, after nine months of fighting that left its old city in ruins. The al-Nuri mosque, where he had preached, had been blown up by ISIS fighters as Iraqi forces closed in.
Raqqa fell that October. In March 2019, at the Syrian village of Baghouz, the self-declared caliphate lost the last of its land.
Al-Baghdadi was still at large. That April, he appeared on video for the first time in nearly five years.

sections.name: The raid
lines: He was hiding in a compound in northwest Syria, close to the Turkish border. On the night of the twenty-sixth of October, 2019, American special forces raided it.
The raid was named after Kayla Mueller, an American aid worker who died in ISIS captivity in 2015. US officials said al-Baghdadi had held her personally.

lines.head: ISIS leader dead in US raid

lines: Cornered in a tunnel, he set off an explosive vest. According to the US military, he killed himself and two young children he had taken with him.

sections.name: Legacy
lines: In Sinjar, families are still searching for the missing, and the dead are still being identified.

His movement did not die with him. As of 2025, Islamic State affiliates remain active in parts of Africa and in Afghanistan, and thousands of former members and their families are still held in camps in Syria.

lines.text: The state fell. The harm did not.

lines: Al-Baghdadi promised a caliphate that would last for ever. It held its cities for barely three years. What lasts far longer is the harm it did: the missing, the bereaved, and the towns still being rebuilt.
